query: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi has high saturation magnetization but a low coercive field, and reported single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys derived from it have coercive fields no greater than 100 Oe in the reported magnetic measurements. What single intervention could overcome this coercivity limitation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted change relative to single-phase fcc FeCoNi or a matched derivative, the relevant compositional, structural, and measurement boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor dopant (≤5 at.%) coupled with a controlled thermal treatment to induce the formation of nanoscale, ordered precipitates (e.g., a B2 or L1₀ phase) within the fcc FeCoNi matrix will significantly increase the coercive field by providing effective domain wall pinning while maintaining high saturation magnetization.
generation.material_initial_state: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy derivative with a coercive field of no more than ~100 Oe and high saturation magnetization.
generation.intervention: Add a small concentration (up to 5 at.%) of a suitable dopant and subject the alloy to a tailored heat-treatment protocol designed to trigger the nucleation of magnetically hard, nanoscale precipitates within the fcc matrix.
generation.conditions: Compositional boundary: dopant content ≤5 at.%; Structural boundary: precipitates must be nanoscale (approximately 5–20 nm) and non-percolating within the fcc matrix; Measurement conditions: ambient temperature magnetic measurements using techniques such as VSM or SQUID, with complementary TEM/XRD analyses for structural verification.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of fine, magnetically hard precipitates embedded in the soft fcc matrix serves as pinning centers for magnetic domain walls.
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates increase the energy barrier for domain wall motion, effectively enhancing the coercive field. They act as obstacles that hinder domain wall displacement when an external magnetic field is applied, thereby requiring a higher field to reverse the magnetization.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coercivity is predicted to increase by at least 50% relative to the baseline (~100 Oe increased to >150 Oe), while the overall high saturation magnetization remains largely unaffected.
generation.baseline: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi and its high-entropy derivatives that exhibit coercivities around 100 Oe with high saturation magnetization.
generation.boundary: The intervention must remain within the fcc-based compositional and structural regime; dopant addition is limited to ≤5 at.%, and the resulting precipitates must be controlled in size (5–20 nm) and distribution. Measurements are to be performed at ambient temperature under standard magnetometry protocols.
generation.uncertainty: While analogous approaches in related alloy systems suggest precipitation-enhanced coercivity, the exact dopant type, optimal concentration, and heat-treatment parameters for this specific system require further optimization. There is uncertainty about the exact magnitude of the coercivity increase until validated experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy samples with incremental dopant additions up to 5 at.%. Subject each sample to an identical controlled heat-treatment designed to promote nanoscale precipitate formation. Use TEM and XRD to verify the presence and size distribution (5–20 nm) of the precipitates, and measure the magnetic properties (coercivity and saturation magnetization) using VSM or SQUID magnetometry at ambient temperature.
measurements: TEM imaging to confirm nanoscale precipitate formation and distribution
XRD for phase identification and confirmation of precipitate phases (e.g., B2 or L1₀)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coercivity fails to increase by at least 50% relative to the baseline (i.e., remains ≤150 Oe) or nano-precipitates are not confirmed by TEM/XRD, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The present work exhibits the effects of Sn addition on the magnetic properties and microstructure of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) high-entropy alloys (HEAs). The results show all the samples consist of a mixed structure of face-centered-cubic (FCC) phase and body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nano-precipitates in BCC matrix. It also shows that the Curie temperatures (Tc) of the FCC phase and the saturation magnetization (Ms) of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs increase greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases after the addition of Sn into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The thermomagnetic curves indicate that the phases of the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs will transform from FCC with low Tc to BCC phase with high Tc at temperature of 600–700 K. This work provides a new idea for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs for their potential application as soft magnets to be used at high temperatures.

Zuo et al. [] found CoNiMnGa HEA shows a low saturation magnetostriction coefficient and a high Curie temperature (Tc). In our previous work [], the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA consisting of BCC and FCC phases shows good magnetic and mechanical properties, and it was found that BCC phases show a higher Ms than that of FCC phases for the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA. The other work of our group [] found a minor amount of Ga addition into FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA can promote the formation of BCC phase and improve the Ms of the alloy, and the value of remanence (Br) and coercivity (Hc) also increases. It was reported that the addition of Sn can hinder the formation of FCC phase [] and promote the formation of BCC phase []. Therefore, in this work, a minor amount of Sn was added into the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 HEA hoping to get a higher volume fraction of BCC phase. In this work, the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs were studied from phase constitutions to microstructure and magnetic properties. It was found that these HEAs show high Ms, low Br, and high Tc, which indicate their potential application as soft magnetic materials. This paper offers a good method for designing future high-performance soft magnet

In this work, the FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs were prepared by vacuum arc-melt casting. Effects of Sn content on the phase constitution and magnetic properties were studied. All the samples are composed of FCC and BCC phases, whereas some unknown phases appear with the addition of Sn. The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nanoprecipitates in the BCC matrix. Moreover, the Ms increases greatly while the remanence (Br) decreases with the increasing of x for FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) HEAs. The addition of Sn can obviously increase the Curie temperature of the FCC phase. The phase of alloys with a mixture of FCC and BCC will transform from FCC to BCC phase at high temperature, leading to an increase of magnetization. They can be used as new soft magnetic materials at high temperatures.

frame.system: Single-phase fcc FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys that demonstrate high saturation magnetization but intrinsically low coercivity (≈100 Oe).
frame.goal: Increase the coercive field (magnetic hardness) of the single-phase fcc FeCoNi system while retaining its high saturation magnetization.
frame.limitation: The inherent low coercivity (no greater than 100 Oe) reported for single-phase fcc FeCoNi or its high-entropy derivatives.
constraints: Only a single intervention is allowed
The alloy must remain compositionally and structurally in the realm of fcc-based FeCoNi derivatives
Intervention must be within the boundaries of composition, structural modification (e.g., micro-/nanoscale phase changes), and measurement conditions similar to previous reports
The experiment needs to include a controlled design with explicit falsification criteria
frame.regime: Magnetic measurements (e.g., using VSM or SQUID magnetometry) at ambient (room) temperature and applied fields typical for characterizing coercivity. The structural regime should be carefully controlled to observe phases on the nanoscale (e.g., via TEM/XRD) to detect secondary phase formations.
prior_attempts: Production of single-phase fcc FeCoNi and its high-entropy derivatives, which reported coercive fields up to ~100 Oe
Conventional alloying routes that preserved the pure fcc structure yet did not achieve significant domain wall pinning necessary for higher coercivity
frame.hypothesis: A viable single intervention is to introduce a controlled nanoscale precipitation of a secondary, magnetically harder phase (e.g., an ordered B2 or L1_0 phase) within the fcc FeCoNi matrix. The mechanism is that these nanoprecipitates will act as effective pinning centers for magnetic domain walls, thereby increasing the energy required to reverse magnetization and boosting the coercive field significantly over the base value (targeting >150 Oe). The intervention would involve the addition of a minor concentration of an element (or a controlled heat-treatment process) that promotes phase separation without drastically altering the overall fcc matrix or reducing the saturation magnetization. This design is bounded by compositional limits (e.g., no more than 5 at.% of the dopant), structural limits ensuring the precipitates remain nanoscale (~5–20 nm) and non-percolating, and measurement boundaries identical to earlier studies (ambient temperature, standardized magnetometry protocols). Prior literature suggests that in similar alloy systems, the introduction of nanoscale hard magnetic precipitates improves coercivity by providing domain wall pinning; thus, if the experiment shows a substantial increase in coercivity (with a falsification criterion being an increase lesser than 50% relative to the single-phase fcc baseline), the intervention would be considered unsuccessful.

decision.trend: Early work focused on producing single‐phase fcc FeCoNi and related high‐entropy alloys where the coercivity was limited to ~100 Oe by virtue of the homogeneous soft magnetic phase. Later studies began to explore the introduction of minor alloying additions (e.g., Sn or Pt) and tailored post‐processing (such as rapid thermal annealing) to promote secondary phase formation. These treatments resulted in the emergence of nanoscale precipitates (for instance, ordered B2 or L10 phases) or mixed-phase architectures that acted as domain wall pinning centers, thereby enhancing coercivity. However, while such approaches have demonstrated that controlled precipitation can increase magnetic hardness, they have not yet been systematically optimized within the strictly fcc compositional/structural regime of FeCoNi derivatives.
decision.unsolved: The challenge remains to achieve a controlled introduction of a magnetically harder precipitate phase within the fcc matrix without compromising the saturation magnetization and overall single-phase character. Specifically, the optimal dopant level and thermal processing parameters to induce a finely dispersed, non-percolating nano-precipitate (capable of effective domain wall pinning) in the FeCoNi system have not been established.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled thermal treatment (with a minor dopant addition of ≤5 at.%) designed to induce the nucleation of nanoscale ordered precipitates (such as a B2 or L10 phase) within the fcc FeCoNi matrix.
decision.why: This approach builds on the trend of using subtle compositional changes combined with precision heat treatments to tailor the microstructure based on previous successes in similar systems (as seen in studies with Sn and Pt additives). The targeted nanoscale precipitates are expected to serve as effective pinning centers for magnetic domain walls, thereby overcoming the inherent low coercivity of single-phase fcc FeCoNi while maintaining a high saturation magnetization.
